Peor
PEE-or
proper noun
Hebrew pē‘ōr, “a cleft” or “opening,” a height in Moab; bound up with Baal-peor, the idol worshipped upon it, and with Israel’s whoredom there.

Biblical Definition

Peor was a height of Moab, “the top of Peor, that looketh toward Jeshimon” (Num 23:28), whither Balak brought Balaam for the third and last attempt to curse Israel. The place is forever bound up with the shame that followed: there Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor, the idol of that mountain, and “the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel” (Num 25:3). The men of Israel went a whoring after the daughters of Moab and Midian, were drawn into the worship of their god, and a plague brake out among the congregation, until Phinehas the son of Eleazar, in holy zeal, turned away the wrath of God. Long after, the elders remember it: “Is the iniquity of Peor too little for us, from which we are not cleansed until this day” (Josh 22:17). Moses charges that the Midianites “beguiled you in the matter of Peor” (Num 25:18), and that the counsel of Balaam wrought this trespass against the LORD (Num 31:16). Here the Scripture names the corruption plainly: idolatry and whoredom, the doubled sin of the high place. Yet the zeal of Phinehas and the swift judgment of God stand as a warning and a mercy. Let the believer flee both idolatry and uncleanness, for the LORD is a jealous God; and let him bless the Mediator whose zeal for His Father’s house, and whose blood, turn away a greater wrath than the plague of Peor.

Webster 1828 Definition

A height in Moab whither Balak brought Balaam, bound up with Baal-peor, Israel’s whoredom, the plague, and the zeal of Phinehas.

PEOR, a height of Moab, the top that looketh toward Jeshimon, whither Balak brought Balaam.

Upon it was worshipped Baal-peor, the idol whose name the mountain bears.

There Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor and went a whoring after the daughters of Moab.

The anger of the LORD was kindled, and a plague brake out, until Phinehas turned away His wrath.

It witnesses against the doubled sin of idolatry and uncleanness, and the jealousy of a holy God.

Key Scripture

Num 23:28 — "And Balak brought Balaam unto the top of Peor, that looketh toward Jeshimon."

Num 25:3 — "And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel."

Num 25:18 — "For they vex you with their wiles, wherewith they have beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, which was slain in the day of the plague for Peor's sake."

Josh 22:17 — "Is the iniquity of Peor too little for us, from which we are not cleansed until this day, although there was a plague in the congregation of the LORD,"

Modern Corruption

A high place of Moab where Israel fell into idolatry and whoredom; Scripture names the doubled sin plainly and sets the zeal of Phinehas against it.

expand to see more

Peor is no mere place-name but the scene of a notorious corruption that Scripture refuses to gloss. Upon this height Baal-peor was worshipped, and there Israel joined himself to the idol and went a whoring after the daughters of Moab (Num 25:3). The dictionary names the sin in Scripture’s own words — idolatry and uncleanness, the wiles of Balaam’s counsel, the trespass that kindled the anger of the LORD and brought a plague upon the camp.

The principle to recover is the jealousy of a holy God and the way of atonement. The plague was stayed not by indulgence but by the zeal of Phinehas, who stood up and executed judgment. So the saint must mortify both idolatry and lust, knowing the LORD will not share His glory; and he must look to the true Mediator, whose zeal and whose blood turn away a wrath greater than the plague of Peor, and cleanse the iniquity from which Israel could not cleanse herself.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for “a cleft” or “opening,” Peor names a height of Moab bound up with the idol Baal-peor.

expand to see more

Peor — Hebrew pē‘ōr, “a cleft” or “opening.”

It was a height of Moab, the top that looketh toward Jeshimon.

Thither Balak brought Balaam for the last attempt to curse Israel.

It bears the name of the idol Baal-peor, worshipped upon its summit.

There Israel fell into idolatry and whoredom, and the plague brake out.

Usage

"Let the believer flee both idolatry and uncleanness, for the LORD at Peor is a jealous God."

"The zeal of Phinehas teaches that holy judgment, not indulgence, turns away the wrath of God."

"A greater Mediator cleanses the iniquity of Peor, from which Israel could not cleanse herself."
